title: Running Programs
subtitle: Build a running routine that leaves room for walking and real life.

blocks.text: A running app may send seventeen alerts before you reach the front door. Your first useful decision is simpler: choose a small session that fits today. Start with walking and add short, comfortable runs when you’re ready.
Become a runner at your own pace.
blocks.detail: Planned walking breaks give you a clear way to control your effort and build running fitness without chasing anyone else’s speed.
blocks.extra: Section 05 gives you a twenty-minute run/walk session to start with.

blocks.text: Running asks your legs to handle repeated landings while your breathing becomes faster. A running program is a planned way to practise that activity over time. It can include walking breaks throughout, even after you gain experience.

Building the ability to keep going longer is called endurance. In this lesson, the starting goal is a manageable session, not a race time. A gentle jog can still feel hard, so a speed that suits someone else may be too much for you.

This is general adult learning, not a personal exercise prescription. Fill out CSEP’s Get Active Questionnaire. A yes answer means follow its extra guidance, not an automatic ban. Keep your answers private.

Start from what you already do comfortably. If regular walking is new, build that habit before adding runs. When you try running, pick a slow pace and short bursts that let you stay in control of your breathing.

Say a sentence out loud as a quick check during these starter sessions. If talking gets hard, slow down or walk instead of forcing the rest of the run. The aim is manageable effort, and running can feel hard even at a slow speed.
Walking breaks belong in the plan. Put them on the timer before starting, so taking one is a choice you expected rather than a decision made under pressure.
Build around your week

Pick two possible run days with a non-running day between them, such as Tuesday and Friday. This is an example, not a required schedule. Keep your other activity easy enough that you don’t arrive at each run already worn out.

Write down your run and walk times, how the session felt and how you felt the next day. Compare with your own recent sessions, not a public leaderboard. Your watch can measure a route. It can’t see the tiring shift you just worked.

Track minutes before distance. A familiar fifteen-minute route is a clearer starting point than trying to match a distance a friend posted online. Many beginner run/walk programs take about 8 to 10 weeks to build up to 30 minutes of steady running, and slower is fine.

items.title: “Walking means the running session failed.”
items.text: A run/walk session is a full session when walking is part of the plan. You can keep this approach for good, instead of making non-stop running the finish line.

blocks.text: Keep equipment simple

Wear comfortable shoes that fit well and aren’t badly worn. Start on a familiar, level route with a clear surface before adding hills. New shoes, new surfaces and more running can each affect your lower legs, so don’t change them all at once.

sections.title: Fictional learning story: The corner bakery

blocks.text: The corner bakery
paragraphs: Darnell, 48, lived in Halifax and wanted to join his sister’s Saturday run/walk outings. Their route ended at the corner bakery, where they caught up before her weekend shift. He missed those talks, but her running pace felt out of reach.

One evening, a running app offered a five-kilometre challenge. Darnell signed up, then tried to run all the way to the harbour without a walking break. He arrived exhausted, turned around early and wondered if Saturday runs were the wrong goal.

His sister offered to meet him closer to home. Darnell still worried she would spend every outing waiting for him, and his work schedule left little time to practise. He had to choose: chase the app’s challenge, or build a session he could repeat.

He chose a short, level loop near his apartment and wrote walking breaks into the plan. On two separate days, he walked first, tried short gentle jogs and walked whenever the effort climbed. He noted which parts felt manageable and didn’t run on the days in between.

Then came a surprise. His sister was coming back from a busy month and wanted more walking herself. Their first Saturday outing became a shared run/walk, with a timer telling them when to walk. Darnell no longer had to wonder whether asking to walk would spoil the morning.

When heavy rain soaked their usual route, they met at an indoor track and did the easier session. Several outings later, Darnell had a routine he was happy to come back to, with no deadline to run farther. They still stopped at the bakery, where the conversation mattered more than any badge.

blocks.text: Choose a goal you control. “Try my planned session twice this week” is easier to act on than “keep up with everyone on Saturday.”
Keep the reason that got you out the door.
blocks.detail: A flexible plan protects the time you care about, whether that’s an outing with someone you love or a quiet break in your week.
blocks.extra: Section 05 shows you how to adjust the session on any day.

blocks.text: The example below is a learning plan for someone who already walks comfortably and is ready to try short runs. It isn’t a medical prescription or an official training plan. Choose an easier version, or get personal advice if it doesn’t suit you.
Example: 20 minutes including walking

items.title: Walk gently for 5 minutes, gradually finding a comfortable rhythm.
Repeat 4 times: jog gently for 30 seconds, then walk for 2 minutes. This middle part takes 10 minutes.
Walk gently for 5 minutes to finish. Total: 20 minutes, including 2 minutes of jogging.

blocks.text: Use a timer and a small loop so you finish near where you started. Keep the jogging relaxed. There’s no sprint or all-out finish. If a run feels too hard, walk that part or end the session early.
An easier version counts. Make the whole session a comfortable walk, or try just one short jog and walk the rest. You don’t owe the timer four repeats.

Repeat this level until it feels manageable during and after several sessions. When you’re ready, change one thing, such as 45-second jogs with the same two-minute walks and four repeats. That makes the session 21 minutes. Keep the pace and number of run days the same.

items.title: “Every runner must increase by ten per cent each week.”
items.text: One percentage can’t judge your readiness. There’s no deadline to move up. Repeat, ease off or get personal advice as needed.

blocks.text: Check how you feel the next day before you change the plan. Unusual tiredness or discomfort is a reason to rethink the next session, not a cue to run more. Pain that builds during runs or lingers the next day, especially in the shins, knees or feet, is a sign to back off and get it checked.

Stop for chest pain or pressure, faintness, or severe or unusual breathlessness. Call 911 for chest pain, fainting, or severe breathing trouble. Pain that changes movement also means stop and seek appropriate advice.

Check local heat and air-quality alerts, and look for ice on your route. Switch to a well-ventilated indoor space, or postpone, when it’s unsafe outside. In short winter days, choose a well-lit route and clothing that helps drivers see you.
Insider tip: Write your easier plan beside the usual one. A paper note can hold both, without announcing that your fitness subscription expires at midnight.
Quick Check

items.title: What is the purpose of planned walking breaks?
items.detail: They help manage effort within the session.

items.title: How much jogging is in the 20-minute example?
Must you advance to the next level each week?
items.text: Repeat or adjust a level according to readiness.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: Jo’s gentle jog makes comfortable speech difficult. What fits this starter approach? A. Run faster to finish sooner. · B. Slow down or walk. · C. Ignore effort until the timer ends.
items.text: Effort guides the starter session; a timer does not override how you feel.

items.title: Sam wants longer runs, more session days and a hill route. What is the better next choice? A. Change all three together. · B. Follow a fixed percentage rule. · C. Consider one small change after manageable sessions.
items.text: Changing one thing makes the new demand easier to judge. There is no required date to progress.

items.title: Ice covers Pat’s usual route. What fits a flexible plan? A. Use a suitable indoor option or postpone. · B. Keep the route to protect an app streak. · C. Run faster to spend less time outside.
items.text: The route must suit current conditions. A streak is not a reason to use unsafe footing.

items.title: Write a brief run/walk session, including the total time and an easier option.
items.text: Walk 5 minutes, then repeat a 30-second jog and 2-minute walk four times, then walk 5 minutes. Total: 20 minutes. My easier option is comfortable walking throughout.

blocks.text: Start with a manageable run/walk plan. Walking breaks remain useful, and repeating an easier level is a valid decision.
Write your own starter plan below, with an easier option for a hard day. If you’re not sure you’re ready, make getting advice your first step.
Check that your plan’s times add up, and decide when you’ll use the easier version.
Keep private screening answers and health details off this sheet. Discuss health questions with an appropriate professional.

items.title: Run/walk
items.text: A session that alternates running and walking.

items.title: Interval
items.text: A planned period of activity before changing pace.

items.title: Endurance
items.text: The ability to keep doing an activity over time.

items.title: Recovery
items.text: Time between harder efforts to rest or move gently.

items.title: Progression
items.text: A gradual change in the demands of your activity.

items.title: Warm-up
items.text: An easy start that prepares you for the session.
